steps.label: Three Ways to Write a Sum
steps.content:
Three Ways to Write a Sum

Think → Pair → ShareWhy might "pre" and "post" be good names for two of these ways?Show the answer

Pre means before and post means after: the operator comes before or after its two values.

An operator is + - * or /. It joins two values. The three ways put the operator in different places.

WayThe operator goesExampleWith brackets
Infixbetween the two values7 - 2(A + B) * C
Prefixbefore the two values- 7 2* + A B C
Postfixafter the two values7 2 -A B + C *
  • All three mean the same sum: 7 - 2.
  • Prefix and postfix never need brackets.
  • Computers like postfix. Next you will see why.

steps.label: Your Turn: Which Way?
steps.content:
Your Turn: Which Way?

Think → Pair → ShareHow can you tell the three ways apart at a glance?Show the answer

Look at where the operators are: between the values, at the front, or at the end.

items.explain: In postfix the operator comes after its two values: 9 4 -.

items.prompt: Which is A * B written in prefix?
items.explain: In prefix the operator comes first, then the values in the same order: * A B.

steps.label: Postfix: Use a Stack
steps.content:
Postfix: Use a Stack

Think → Pair → ShareWhy must the first number popped go on the right?Show the answer

It was pushed last, so it was written last. The number written first always goes on the left.

A stack is a pile. You push a number onto the top. You pop a number off the top.

  • Read from left to right.
  • A number: push it.
  • An operator: pop two numbers, work them out, push the answer.
  • The first number popped goes on the right.
  • At the end one number is left: the answer.

Game 1: Stack Stacker

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is the answer always the last number left on the stack?Show the answer

Every operator turns two numbers into one. When the last operator is done, only the answer is left.

Push or pop at each token, then type each answer. A mistake costs a heart. Win 2 rounds to go up a level.

steps.label: Prefix: Read from the Right
steps.content:
Prefix: Read from the Right

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do we read prefix from the right?Show the answer

Each operator comes before its numbers. Reading from the right, its numbers are already on the stack when we reach it.

Prefix uses the same stack. Read it the other way.

  • Read from right to left.
  • A number: push it.
  • An operator: pop two numbers, work them out, push the answer.
  • The first number popped goes on the left.

steps.label: Your Turn: Prefix
steps.content:
Your Turn: Prefix

Think → Pair → ShareIn prefix, why does the first number popped go on the left?Show the answer

We read from the right, so the left number is pushed last. The last one pushed is the first one popped.

Read from the right. Use the stack on paper.

Total: 2 marks

steps.label: Infix to Postfix and Prefix
steps.content:
Infix to Postfix and Prefix

Think → Pair → ShareWhy put brackets round every operation first?Show the answer

Then each operator has its own pair of brackets, so you know exactly which two values it joins.

Three steps. Remember: * and / are worked out before + and -.

  1. Put brackets round every operation, in the order you work it out.
  2. Move each operator to the end (postfix) or the front (prefix) of its own brackets.
  3. Remove the brackets.
Infix: A + B * CPostfixPrefix
1. Brackets(A + (B * C))(A + (B * C))
2. Move(A (B C *) +)(+ A (* B C))
3. RemoveA B C * ++ A * B C

steps.label: Bit Strings: NOT, AND, OR, XOR
steps.content:
Bit Strings: NOT, AND, OR, XOR

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can you work out AND, OR and XOR one column at a time?Show the answer

Each column only uses the two bits in that column. No column changes another one.

A bit string is a row of bits, like 10110. Work one column at a time. XOR is new.

NOT

  • The answer has the same number of bits.
  • XOR: 1 and 0 give 1. Two the same give 0.

steps.label: Game 2: Bit Switch Board
steps.content:
Game 2: Bit Switch Board

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the board give you only one check?Show the answer

So you work out every bit before you check, as in the contest, and do not just try switches until it works.

Flip the switches to show the answer, then press Check. One check each round. Win 2 rounds to go up a level.

steps.label: Shifts and Circulates
steps.content:
Shifts and Circulates

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a shift bring in a 0, but a circulate does not?Show the answer

A shift loses the bit that falls off, so a 0 fills the gap. A circulate puts that same bit in the gap.

These move every bit one place. The number after the dash says how many places.

Start: 10011

start10011
LSHIFT-100110
RSHIFT-101001
LCIRC-100111
RCIRC-111001
  • Shift (LSHIFT, RSHIFT): the bit that falls off is lost. A 0 comes in at the other end.
  • Circulate (LCIRC, RCIRC): the bit that falls off comes back at the other end.
  • LSHIFT-2 moves 2 places: do LSHIFT-1 twice.
  • The answer always has the same number of bits.

steps.label: Game 3: Shift Switch Board
steps.content:
Game 3: Shift Switch Board

Think → Pair → ShareIn a two-step question, why do you work out the brackets first?Show the answer

The operator outside the brackets works on the answer of the brackets, so that answer must come first.

The same board with shifts and circulates. Level 4 has two steps: set both rows. One check each round.

steps.label: FOR Loops in Contest Code
steps.content:
FOR Loops in Contest Code

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the loop stop after i = 4?Show the answer

After i = 4, NEXT makes i = 5. That is past the end number 4, so the loop stops.

01  c = 0
02  FOR i = 1 TO 4
03      c = c + 2
04  NEXT i
05  OUTPUT c
  • FOR i = 1 TO 4 gives i the values 1, 2, 3, 4.
  • The lines between FOR and NEXT run once for each value.
  • STEP 2 adds 2 each time: FOR i = 1 TO 9 STEP 2 gives 1, 3, 5, 7, 9.
  • OUTPUT c shows the value of c.

Game 4: Loop Runner

Predicting makes you trace the loop yourself. The run then shows if your trace was right.
